name: Thick pork chops
tile_uses: The weekend meal, the charred plate, fig toast
why_now: Pork isn't more in season in August — but stone fruit is, and pork with ripe, charred fruit is one of the oldest pairings there is. A thick chop also cooks in ten minutes, which is the right amount of time to spend at a hot stove in August.
how_to_choose: Bone-in and at least an inch thick — thin chops overcook before they brown
Pink to light red, not gray
A good band of white fat along the edge
Firm and dry on the surface, not sitting in liquid
buy_this_much: 2 chops. One for the weekend meal, one for later in the week.
price_note: Ask the butcher counter to cut them thick if the case only has thin ones. They will.

flavor_paths.name: Seared
flavor_paths.description: Salted early, hot pan, rested. The weekend meal.

weekday_uses: Sliced and warmed for the charred plate
Over a rice bowl with jalapeño and lime
weekend_use: Salted early, seared hard, rested, with nectarines charred in the same pan. The weekend meal.
storage: Cook within two days of buying. Salted and uncovered in the fridge, they're better on day two than day one.
one_thing_to_learn: Modern pork is safe and juiciest at 140–145°F — slightly pink at the center. Most people cook it to 160°F out of habit, which is why they think pork chops are dry.
market_question: Can you cut these an inch and a quarter thick?
